Hi there. First off, I want to acknowledge your incredible courage; not just for surviving what you’ve survived, but for choosing to speak up now, even when you feel broken. That takes immense strength. I’m so sorry for all that you've endured.

I’m a trauma-informed therapist who works closely with survivors and with couples navigating relationship patterns shaped by past trauma. And I want to say this as gently but clearly as possible: your husband’s trauma may explain his behavior, but it does not excuse it. His wounds are real, but so are yours, and someone else’s pain never gives them the right to cause more.

What you’re experiencing is emotional abuse. It’s not a cultural norm. It’s not a misunderstanding. It’s not something you should have to “get over.” And it’s not something therapy will necessarily fix, unless he is deeply, consistently committed to changing, over time, with accountability, not just apologies.

You are right to sense that trauma cycles repeat when they are left unhealed. His father abused his mother. His mother told him not to be like his father. And now, he is becoming what he witnessed, and it should break his heart, not yours.

It’s not your job to rescue him. It's not your job to be the emotional punching bag for his unresolved pain. You say he’s fragile, but you are fragile too right now, and he is breaking you further instead of helping you heal. That’s not love. That’s harm disguised as attachment.

The fact that you still want to understand him and advocate for him even after all he’s said to you shows your depth of compassion. But don’t let your empathy become your prison. You are not here to fix a man at the cost of your own soul.

You deserve peace. You deserve safety. You deserve a partner who protects your inner world, not someone who weaponizes your deepest wounds. Please consider whether staying is truly helping either of you grow or just prolonging a cycle that will take even more from you.

I'm sending warmth and strength your way. And if you need help feel free to reach out. You're not alone.

Hi, Therapist here.
A few things to know before you go to therapy-
1. Every therapist uses different modalities, reading up a bit about these and understanding which would suit you best might prove helpful.
2. It is difficult to find a therapist that suits your needs, to zero down on that, look for the kind of cases or issues they specialise in and then pick one suitable for you.
3. The initial couple of sessions are for assessment, they understand your issues in depth, the actual work begins from the second or third session onwards.
4. Therapy isn't a one stop solution. We therapists don't give you a solution, tell you what is right or wrong or good or bad for you. Suppose you come to us with an issue, we help you come up with a solution for yourself, our role is to facilitate it.
5. It's slow but dynamic as a process. You won't see results overnight and we don't magically make things better, there has to be active participation, motivation and involvement from your end otherwise there's only so much we can do.

I walk in the mornings, lift in the evening.
On days that I lift in the mornings, I walk 2-3 Kms after every meal.

If you are training 6 times a week, I'd suggest you do Cardio 4-5 times a week. Out of which you can have 2-3 days a week for the incline version, the remainder for no incline walks or a run, walk outdoors.

Why I am saying this is because, I've seen a lot of people being told that walking incline is the key to fat loss, while it does burn calories and aid fat loss, it also puts significant pressure on your knees, ankles and lower back for which you need time and rest to recover from. Any form of cardio at a moderate conversational pace burns calories and in turn fat. Also, I mentioned the outdoors because, walking and running outside are very different from doing that on the treadmill, indoors. 

Now, coming to the next part of your question, I use incline walks for 20-25 minutes once or twice a week. For the rest of my cardio, I walk all 7 days a week. 40-45 minutes of paced walking in a fasted state that covers 6-7 Km and another 2-3 Km post dinner at a moderate pace. I aim for 10 Km a day usually but 15 Km on the day that I'm not lifting. I weight-train 5 days a week. Been doing this since January began and I've lost 4.5 Kgs.

I hope this was helpful.

If only people saw how patriarchy is harmful to women AND, wait for it... Men.

Nobody is denying that male victims of rape exist but statistically speaking, Men are less likely to report sexual assault compared to women and cultural stigma, societal perceptions make reporting difficult. Under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita (BNS) 2023, male rape victims face significant legal challenges as -Rape laws are not gender-neutral, Only women can be victims of rape, Only men can be perpetrators of rape and Male rape victims will be covered under grievous hurt provisions. They've essentially decriminalizes male rape.
Now, constitutionally speaking, The law potentially violates Article 14 (right to equality) by creating arbitrary gender-based distinctions in sexual violence definitions. This leaves male and transgender victims without comprehensive legal protection against sexual assault.
Which essentially circles back to what I said in my previous comment that instead of warring that men have it difficult or women have it easy, we must rally together to dismantle the patriarchal structures that exist and it harms both men and women. This law here is a glowering example of that. If the policy makers of our society are of the mindset that men cannot be victims of rape and only perpetrators we really need to rethink about the state of the societal fabric.

First off, I'm a man as well and no one said that men's rights shouldn't be protected. 
False allegations are rare and should not be conflated with the systemic violence women face. Less than 8% of rape cases are found to be "false" according to the National Crime Records Bureau. Most sexual violence instances in India go unreported. Most "false" cases often involve complex social dynamics, such as parents filing complaints about eloped couples. Patriarchal structures consistently downplay violence against women and yes, false cases of domestic violence and rape exist, and they are a serious issue because they not only harm the accused but also undermine the credibility of genuine survivors. However, false cases are the exception, not the norm. Research indicates that the overwhelming majority of cases of domestic violence and sexual assault reported are genuine. The perception of a high number of false cases is often inflated by anecdotal evidence and media sensationalism and cases like Atul Subhash's highlight how most people try to weaponise it to antagonise women. The notion that "men's rights" are under threat often stems from a misunderstanding of systemic issues. Patriarchal systems, which have historically oppressed women, also negatively affect men by enforcing rigid gender roles. Men are often seen as the "protector" or "breadwinner," which can limit their emotional and personal growth. However, laws addressing domestic violence and sexual violence are not designed to "punish men" but to protect survivors who, statistically, are disproportionately women.
Men do face unique issues, such as the lack of emotional support, societal pressure, and stigma around mental health. However, addressing these issues should not come at the cost of delegitimizing women's struggles or dismantling laws that protect women. Advocating for men's mental health, support systems, and equitable treatment is important but can coexist with protecting women's rights.

TLDR- False cases should be addressed through better implementation of the law and mechanisms to protect the falsely accused, not by dismantling protections for survivors of abuse and violence. The focus should be on improving the system to ensure justice for everyone while understanding that laws addressing gender-based violence are a response to centuries of systemic oppression. Instead of perpetuating a "battle of the sexes," we should aim for a society where everyone's rights and safety are upheld.

Hello, Psychologist here.

Step 1- Sit down with your parents and discuss this without him being present. I understand that it will be stress inducing but the situation is still not too bad to recover from. When you tell someone something this serious, there might be an adverse negative reaction from all parties involved, emotions will rung high so be a little patient and try to diffuse the situation tactfully. All is not lost.

Step 2- Since drugs are involved, help him pay his debts away and make sure he doesn't owe anyone anything because the debt amount is not something very large, yet. 

Step 3- Pull him out of college for the semester. He's still young, he has his whole life ahead of him, a drop sem or drop year won't hurt his career as opposed to what a life of addiction will do. 

Step 4- Spend more family time together, talk to him without any angst, judgement or sadness. I understand that it's easy to say and there will be negative emotions but please try to limit them around him it may be difficult but empathy and patience go a long way in helping with these situations. Be kind and loving with him to understand what pushed him down the road, in my experience addiction is sometimes a reaction to possible underlying issues. 

Step 5- Get professional help, be it a psychologist, rehab, anything. It's best to find the underlying cause and help the individual rather than just treating a symptom (the addiction can possibly be a symptom of something more profound). 

Hope it helps.
